title: Genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 in Tunisia during the omicron era: insights from the national influenza & other respiratory viruses laboratory

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to fill the gap in understanding SARS-CoV-2 lineage dynamics and genomic surveillance performance in North Africa, particularly in Tunisia, during the omicron era. The research addressed the need for more comprehensive genomic surveillance data in the region.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 in Tunisia from November 2021 to September 2025, using samples from a national sentinel network. The surveillance included 8,635 nasopharyngeal swabs, of which 1,020 (11.8%) were positive for SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.methods: Samples were tested for SARS-CoV-2 by real-time RT-PCR, and 669 positive samples were sequenced using Illumina RNA Prep with Enrichment and a respiratory virus panel. Sequencing coverage, geographic representativeness, turnaround times, temporal trends, lineage diversity, mutational profiles, and phylogenetic placement were summarized descriptively.
analysis.main_results: The overall SARS-CoV-2 positivity rate was 11.8%. Among the sequenced samples, 92 (13.8%) showed co-detection with other respiratory viruses, including influenza. The most prevalent lineages were XBB* (25.0%), BA.4/BA.5* (22.1%), JN.1* and descendants (13.6%), BA.2* (12.6%), and BA.1* (9.0%). Delta represented 8.7% of genomes, and the remaining 9.1% belonged to other lineages, including pre-Omicron variants and non-XBB recombinants.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study captured rapid Omicron sublineage turnover and co-detections with other respiratory viruses, including influenza, through genomic monitoring integrated into Tunisia's influenza-based sentinel network. This approach achieved broad sequencing coverage and overall near-proportional sampling despite subnational heterogeneity, providing a scalable model for sustained genomic surveillance and future respiratory pandemic preparedness.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for SARS-CoV-2 in Tunisia and similar regions, highlighting the importance of integrated multi-pathogen approaches for genomic surveillance and pandemic preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include potential sampling biases due to subnational heterogeneity and the reliance on a sentinel network, which may not capture all cases. The evidence strength is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 in Tunisia from 2021 to 2025, capturing rapid Omicron sublineage turnover and co-detections with other respiratory viruses. The approach provided broad sequencing coverage and near-proportional sampling, offering a scalable model for future surveillance and pandemic preparedness.

title: COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness in people on immunosuppressive therapies: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

analysis.research_question_and_background: People on immunosuppressive therapies are at increased risk of severe COVID-19, yet vaccine efficacy in these individuals has been inadequately assessed in randomised controlled trials.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to examine vaccine effectiveness in people with medical conditions commonly treated with conventional synthetic or targeted immunosuppressive therapies. We included randomised controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies of COVID-19 vaccines in adults with haematological malignancies or autoimmune and immune-mediated inflammatory disorders.
analysis.methods: We searched PubMed and Scopus from database inception and Embase from Jan 1, 2020, until Dec 5, 2025. We excluded studies of organ transplant recipients and patients with other conditions (eg, HIV or non-haematologic cancers). Data were extracted by one author (SRK or ES) and verified by another author (SRK, KME, ES, CP, PH, RVH, RVJ, or SCS). Risk of bias was assessed independently by two authors (KME and EE) using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Effect measures were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with inverse variance weighting.
analysis.main_results: Our database search identified 3316 studies, and one additional study was identified from citation searching. 35 studies were eligible for inclusion in the review, of which 34 were included in the meta-analysis (one study was excluded due to no cases in all arms). Of the 34 included studies, 17 reported vaccine effectiveness against COVID-19 outcomes in people on immunosuppressive therapies compared with unvaccinated individuals, 16 reported RR measures in vaccinated individuals on immunosuppressive therapies compared with vaccinated healthy controls, and one reported both.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This analysis shows a substantial benefit of vaccination for people on immunosuppressive therapy, particularly after three vaccine doses and against severe outcomes. It also highlights a significantly higher risk of hospitalisation and death in this group than in vaccinated healthy individuals.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings cautiously inform the importance of vaccination for people on immunosuppressive therapies, particularly in reducing the risk of severe outcomes. Assessing booster vaccine effectiveness in these populations against current circulating variants and with updated vaccines remains a priority.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design, but the risk of bias was rated as good in 62% of the studies, fair in 12%, and poor in 26%. The evidence strength is moderate due to the heterogeneity of the included studies and the potential for bias.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines in individuals on immunosuppressive therapies, a population at higher risk for severe disease. The study included randomised controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies of vaccines in adults with haematological malignancies or autoimmune and immune-mediated inflammatory disorders. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, and Embase was conducted, and 35 studies were eligible for inclusion, with 34 included in the meta-analysis. The results showed vaccine effectiveness of 82·3% (95% CI 72·4-88·7) against SARS-CoV-2 infection with pre-omicron variants after three vaccinations and 88·4% (82·8-92·3) against hospitalisation. Among vaccinated individuals on immunosuppressive therapies, the relative risk compared with vaccinated healthy individuals was 1·57 (1·25-1·96) for infection, 3·72 (1·63-8·47) for hospitalisation, and 3·14 (1·51-6·54) for death. The authors interpreted these findings as demonstrating a substantial benefit of vaccination for people on immunosuppressive therapy, particularly against severe outcomes, while also highlighting a significantly higher risk of hospitalisation and death in this group compared to vaccinated healthy individuals. The study's evidence strength is moderate due to the heterogeneity of the included studies and the potential for bias.

title: COVID-19 mortality risk among people with HIV in Florida before and after the introduction of COVID-19 vaccines: A population-based study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess associations between the availability of COVID-19 vaccines and differences in mortality risk among people with HIV (PWH) in Florida, addressing the need to understand how vaccine access might influence outcomes in this subgroup during the pandemic.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed HIV surveillance data, Social Vulnerability Index (SVI), and Rural-Urban Commuting Area Codes from 122,527 people with HIV in Florida, comparing mortality rates before and during the vaccine availability period (March 1, 2020–April 30, 2021 and May 1, 2021–December 31, 2021, respectively).
analysis.methods: A competing risks model was used to compare mortality rates among people with HIV before and during the vaccine availability period, incorporating data from HIV surveillance, SVI, and Rural-Urban Commuting Area Codes.
analysis.main_results: Overall COVID-19 mortality rates increased from 22.3 to 27.5 per 100,000 person-months during the vaccine availability period, driven by the Delta variant surge. Adjusted mortality hazards remained elevated for Non-Hispanic Black PWH both before and during vaccine availability, with HRs of 2.06 (95% CI 1.45-2.91) and 1.60 (95% CI 1.13-2.27), respectively. For Hispanic PWH, the relative hazard compared to Non-Hispanic White PWH was elevated before vaccine availability (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.55-3.23) but attenuated during (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.68-1.57). Living in ZIP Code-level areas of high social vulnerability was associated with elevated hazard during vaccine availability (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.04-2.97).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that subgroup patterns of mortality varied substantially, with inequities persisting among key subgroups, particularly those in socially vulnerable areas, highlighting the need for targeted interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the importance of tailored vaccination strategies and structural interventions to address disparities in mortality risk among people with HIV during the pandemic, particularly in socially vulnerable communities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is observational and does not estimate the causal effect of vaccination uptake, which limits the strength of the evidence. However, the use of a competing risks model and comprehensive data sources provides a moderate level of confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of COVID-19 vaccine availability on mortality risk among people with HIV in Florida, comparing outcomes before and during the vaccine rollout period. It found that overall mortality rates increased during the vaccine availability period, driven by the Delta variant surge. Mortality hazards remained elevated for Non-Hispanic Black PWH both before and during vaccine availability, while Hispanic PWH showed a reduction in relative hazard during the period. Social vulnerability was also linked to higher mortality risk. The study highlights persistent inequities and underscores the need for targeted strategies to improve outcomes among vulnerable subgroups. However, the observational nature of the study limits causal inference.

title: Maternal mortality in pregnant women with COVID-19 during the early pandemic period (2019–2022): a systematic review of published cases

analysis.scope_and_question: Pregnant women were at higher risk for Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), and this infection can lead to adverse effects such as maternal mortality, preterm delivery, and miscarriage. This study aimed to report maternal mortality in pregnant women with COVID-19 and how COVID-19 is related to their death, clinical features, and laboratory changes.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We conducted a systematic search on PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, and Embase to identify studies addressing maternal mortality and COVID-19 in pregnancy during 2019–2022. The following terms were used: [“maternal mortality”] AND [“COVID-19” OR “SARS-CoV-2” OR “2019-nCoV”]. Fourteen relevant research articles were included in our study.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The highest maternal mortality rate due to COVID-19 was reported in the third trimester and postpartum, with 133 mothers (133/172). Cardiopulmonary complications caused by SARS-CoV-2 were identified as leading cause of maternal death. Based on the results of the current study, it is evident that COVID-19 and its complications played a significant role in maternal mortality in pregnant women during the early pandemic period (2019–2022).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: There has been limited information available about COVID-19 in pregnancy. These findings reflect an era before widespread vaccination and population immunity. Further studies examining maternal outcomes in the post-vaccination era are strongly recommended.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Since 2022, the emergence of new variants (e.g., Omicron) and high vaccination coverage have substantially altered COVID-19 severity in pregnancy. These results should be interpreted as historical baseline data rather than current risk estimates.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review analyzed maternal mortality in pregnant women with COVID-19 during the early pandemic period (2019–2022). It found that the highest maternal mortality rate was observed in the third trimester and postpartum, with 133 out of 172 cases. Cardiopulmonary complications were the leading cause of death. The study highlights the significant role of COVID-19 in maternal mortality during this time, emphasizing that these findings represent historical baseline data before widespread vaccination. The review recommends further studies to assess maternal outcomes in the post-vaccination era, as new variants and vaccination have altered the disease's impact on pregnancy.

title: ACE2 dysregulation and lipid metabolism: Mechanistic interplay between COVID-19 and neurodegeneration

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on SARS-CoV-2, specifically examining the interplay between ACE2 regulation, lipid metabolism, and systemic inflammation in the context of COVID-19 and its neurological implications. It addresses the role of ACE2 as the primary receptor for SARS-CoV-2 and its involvement in modulating inflammatory pathways and blood pressure. The central question is how these mechanisms contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, particularly in patients with Long COVID.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of existing literature, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It includes general background information on ACE2 and lipid metabolism, as well as results from studies linking dyslipidaemia to severe COVID-19 and Long COVID. The review does not report on study counts or eligibility criteria.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that ACE2 dysregulation and lipid metabolism alterations are interconnected and play a significant role in the pathophysiology of severe COVID-19 and Long COVID. It highlights that these factors may contribute to neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier impairment, potentially exacerbating or accelerating neurodegenerative processes. The review also notes that understanding these mechanisms is essential for preventing long-term neurological consequences of the pandemic.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies a lack of comprehensive studies on the specific mechanisms linking ACE2 and lipid metabolism to neurodegenerative diseases. It also notes that while dyslipidaemia is associated with increased susceptibility to severe COVID-19, the exact causal relationship and its impact on neurological outcomes remain unclear. Additionally, the review acknowledges that the role of lipid rafts in ACE2 localization and viral entry is not fully understood.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that future research should focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which ACE2 and lipid metabolism interact in the context of SARS-CoV-2 infection and Long COVID. It also recommends exploring therapeutic strategies targeting ACE2 and lipid metabolism to mitigate acute infection, systemic inflammation, and persistent neurological sequelae. Furthermore, it highlights the need for improved surveillance and diagnostic tools to identify patients at risk for these complications.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the interplay between ACE2 regulation, lipid metabolism, and systemic inflammation in SARS-CoV-2 infection and its neurological consequences. It highlights that ACE2, the primary receptor for SARS-CoV-2, modulates inflammatory pathways and blood pressure, and its function is influenced by the lipid composition of the plasma membrane. Dyslipidaemia, common in metabolic disorders, is linked to increased susceptibility to severe COVID-19 and Long COVID, which may contribute to neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative processes. The review underscores the importance of understanding these mechanisms to develop targeted interventions and prevent long-term neurological effects of the pandemic.

title: SARS-CoV-2 and RSV external quality assessment on molecular detection and variant typing in European expert laboratories in 2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the diagnostic capabilities of European expert public health laboratories for SARS-CoV-2 and RSV, addressing the need for reliable and consistent diagnostic testing during the pandemic and beyond.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved 37 laboratories from 32 European countries, investigating SARS-CoV-2 and RSV detection and variant typing through a wet-lab external quality assessment (EQA) organized by the AURORAE consortium.
analysis.methods: A 10-sample panel was produced and validated, containing various SARS-CoV-2 variants, RSV lineages, a common cold coronavirus, and a negative control. Laboratories were invited by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) to submit results and assay details via electronic forms.
analysis.main_results: Thirty-seven laboratories from 32 European countries participated. SARS-CoV-2 was correctly identified by 23 laboratories (62%), while RSV groups were correctly determined by 20 laboratories (54%). Thirteen laboratories successfully generated SARS-CoV-2 sequences, and only two obtained RSV sequences.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study showed that molecular detection of SARS-CoV-2 within Europe has improved over time, with commercial assays being the most commonly used. However, challenges remain in detecting RSV samples with low viral load and identifying lineages for low-concentration specimens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of routine monitoring of diagnostic and surveillance assays via EQAs to maintain accurate and reliable testing, especially as the diagnostic panel broadens to include other respiratory viruses like RSV.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the reliance on voluntary participation, which may introduce bias, and the focus on molecular detection rather than other diagnostic methods. The evidence strength is moderate due to the voluntary nature of participation and the limited number of RSV sequences obtained.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the diagnostic capabilities of European laboratories for SARS-CoV-2 and RSV through an EQA, showing improved molecular detection but challenges in low-viral-load samples. Routine EQAs are crucial for maintaining reliable testing.

title: Assessing SARS-CoV-2 immune markers in vaccinated asymptomatic adults after household exposure in Canada (AB-PROTECT): a prospective cohort study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate antibody and T-cell immune markers against SARS-CoV-2 infection among household contacts of index patients infected with SARS-CoV-2. Determining the early immune response against SARS-CoV-2 in vaccinated individuals is essential for better understanding immune memory and informing COVID-19 vaccine design and use.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective observational cohort study was conducted on vaccinated and asymptomatic adult household contacts of outpatients who presented to the Emergency Department or COVID-19 Assessment Centre at Michael Garron Hospital with a SARS-CoV-2 infection in Toronto, ON, Canada. Participants were followed up for 28 days with repeat testing for SARS-CoV-2 infection and serological assessments.
analysis.methods: Blood specimens were collected to measure SARS-CoV-2 anti-spike and anti-receptor-binding domain (RBD) IgG and IgA antibodies and to conduct SARS-CoV-2 spike-pseudotyped neutralisation assays, live SARS-CoV-2 microneutralisation assays, and assessments of CD4 + and CD8 + T-cell activation and functional cytokine responses to SARS-CoV-2 proteins. T-cell responses were assessed in a convenience subset of participants starting Jan 19, 2022.
analysis.main_results: Of 484 participants enrolled, 432 had sufficient follow-up information for final analysis. SARS-CoV-2 infection developed in 210 (49%) of 432 participants, of whom 182 (87%) developed symptoms. No change was seen in the probability of infection between the 10th and 90th percentiles of anti-spike IgG levels or anti-RBD IgG levels. The predicted probability decreased by 3% for pseudoneutralisation capacity against ancestral SARS-CoV-2 and by 5% for live-virus microneutralisation titres. Participants with infection had enhanced Th17 CD4 + T-cell activation responses to SARS-CoV-2 membrane protein stimulation early after household exposure.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Early after household exposure, binding and neutralising antibodies were similar in all participants, but differences in T-cell functional responses were evident in individuals who developed symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that early T-cell responses may be important in the early immune response to SARS-CoV-2 infection, particularly in symptomatic individuals. This could inform future vaccine design and use.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the observational nature of the design and the potential for confounding factors. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and the potential for selection bias.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated antibody and T-cell immune markers in vaccinated asymptomatic adults after household exposure to SARS-CoV-2. While early antibody levels were similar, T-cell responses differed between those who developed symptoms and those who remained asymptomatic.
